en: Title: Rūdrayāmalatantra-paramahaṃsapaddhatiḥ; Extent: 8 [units]

Subject: Tantra, page 1a) Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Oṃ Haṃsaḥ. Oṃ Tat Sat! I take refuge in that which is Consciousness, Bliss, and the Supreme Self, which is beyond the reach of thought and free from the rising of duality. Oṃ Haṃsaḥ. Oṃ. Of this mantra of the venerable Guru, the Supreme Self as the deity: Jñānasāgara is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of pleasing the deity, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, the Paramahaṃsa. Now, the ritual assignment of the hands (*karanyāsa*): Oṃ Hmau Sauḥ, salutation to both thumbs; Saṃ, salutation to both index fingers; Śaṃ, salutation to both middle fingers; Śaṃ, salutation to both ring fingers; Śaṃ, salutation to both little fingers; Saṃ, salutation to both palms and backs of the hands. Thus ends the ritual assignment of the hands.

Now, the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): *Śaṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *Śaṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *Śaṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *Śaṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *Śaṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *Śaṃ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Thus ends the ritual placement of the six limbs. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[One meditates upon Him] whose body is stainless and pure, the singular light, the manifestation, the source, whose nature is pure witness-consciousness, existence, consciousness, and bliss. Equal...
I bow to you, the true Guru, whose nature is rasa, who is security, eternal bliss, and the abode of all worlds.

(1) One should recite the mantra one thousand times, or likewise one hundred and eight times; thereafter, having gone outside, one should perform the acts of purification. (2) Having gone toward the north to a secluded place free from people, [one should discharge] excrement and urine into a vessel or cloth. Om, Om, Utthi... (3)

O you who are self-existent, the protector of those who have become [liberated] from the six states; I shall void excrement and urine—may no fault be attributed to me. A wise person should recite this mantra for the removal of excrement and urine according to their capacity: *Moṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ svāhā*. At the conclusion, one should perform the proper purificatory rites (*saucācāra*).

One application of clay for the penis, three for the anus, seven for the hands and feet, and seven applications of clay [for the body]; this is the purification for a householder. For a student (brahmacārī), it is twofold; for a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), threefold; and for yogis, fourfold. Five applications for the private parts, seven for the hands, and eleven for the feet. Having taken water and clay, one should wash with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). And the conch...
Having joyfully proclaimed this mudrā of the blood-drinking lotus, I shall now explain that method, specifically the mantras.

The bow, the womb, the conch, and the protective jar-seal; (4) all these specific characteristics for the sipping of water (*ācamana*) and so forth are purifying from the water. One should perform two, three, or six *gaṇḍūṣas* (mouthfuls), and then wash both hands and feet. (5) Having performed one *gaṇḍūṣa*, the wise man should indeed perform the sipping (*ācamana*) and the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and then wash the vessel with earth mixed with water.

6. Once, perform the washing of the vessel twenty-one times. Taking water in the palm of the hand, perform the washing of the vessel. 7. One should take seven mouthfuls of water (gaṇḍūṣa) as before and recite the Praṇava. The characteristic of the tooth-stick is that it should be twelve finger-breadths in length. 8. Having washed the mouth, one should place the vessel of holy water (tīrtha-pātra) there, accompanied by the Praṇava recited ten times.

Then the wise man should perform the purification of the staff (*daṇḍa-śauca*), the purification of *Caitra*, as well as the purification of the person (*pumān-śauca*), the sipping of water (*ācamana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the assignment of directions (*digbandhana*), and the sixteen-fold filling (*ṣoḍaśāṃ pūrayet*).

A man should perform sixty-four *kuṃbhaka* (retentions) and thirty-two *recakas* (exhalations). This is the definition of *prāṇāyāma*. *Oṃ*, salutations to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, Viṣṇu, to Brahmā in the *praṇava*, and to Śiva.

Having bowed to the lineage of gurus up to the *diguru*, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the teeth (*dantadhāvana*) and then proceed with the waist-bath (*kaṭisnāna*). With the twenty-one-fold mantra, one should take earth mixed with water. Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and bowed to the lineage of gurus up to the *diguru*, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu and Śiva.
Having placed the water for sipping (*ācamana*) upon an eight-petaled lotus, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and the Sarasvatī.

*Svati* [said]: "Having come to this place, I shall perform purification. One should apply clay twenty-one times to the arms, the anus, the hands, the forehead, and the head. Having bathed with the root mantra, one should likewise perform sixteen face-baths. Then, having performed *ācamana* (sipping water) and *prāṇāyāma* (breath control), one should offer an *arghya* (water oblation) to the Sun along with the six limbs [of the mantra]. Oṃ ghraṃ ghriṃ para..."
"O Self, O Deity, accept this water-offering (arghya); grant me success! Svāhā to the Sun!"—thus I offer five times. (pṛ0 2ba) [Then follows:

The sipping of water (ācamana), the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and the meditation on the Self (brahma-svayaṃ-dhyāna), which consists of the letters beginning with 'Va' and ending with 'Sa', together with the letter 'Ra', and is considered supreme; likewise, that which consists of the letters beginning with 'Va' and ending with 'Sa', together with the letter 'Ra', and is considered supreme.

Oṃ haṃsa paramahaṃsa brahma oṃ *tattvamasi* oṃ. Haṃso ’haṃ sat-tattvamasi oṃ. Haṃso ’haṃ sat-tattvamasi oṃ. Ahaṃ brahmāsmi, ahaṃ brahma tattvamasi, tat so ’haṃ paramahaṃsaḥ. This is the mantra of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*). Oṃ (haṃsaḥ so ’haṃ).

So ’haṃ haṃsaḥ, the Supreme Self, consisting of consciousness; whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss—so ’haṃ brahma. Thus is the mantra. [The rite of] sipping water (*ācamana*)... *Note: The asterisk indicates the standard Sanskrit term for "thou art that. The text provided contains some orthographic variations and repetitions.*

The Procedure for Nyāsa: Oṃ. Of this mantra of the Śrī Mātṛkā-nyāsa, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in the form of the Guru, the Paramahaṃsa, is the deity (devatā). Its application (viniyoga) is in recitation (japa) for the sake of attaining all perfections (siddhis). Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ. [These are placed] on the circle of the face. Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ. [These are placed] on the five fingers of the right hand.
*Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ* in the five joints of the left hand; *oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ* in the joints of the right foot;

*oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ* in the joints of the left foot; *oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ* in the abdomen; *oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ* in the heart; *oṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ* in the head; *oṃ laṃ kṣaṃ* in all the limbs. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): *Oṃ*, [in the center] of the lotus of the heart...

The reflection of the Self (Ātman) is impermanent; it is the seed within the entire body and the cause of all worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). It becomes the form of a swan (*haṃsa*) with stainless and pure luster, appearing as the web of existence while being the nature of consciousness and the Self. Having prayed by reciting "I am That" (*so'ham*) as the ritual pin (*kīlaka*) and "Salutation to the feet," one should perform the rite, for the Earth is the Supreme Brahman. *Oṃ*, of this glorious Nārāyaṇa in the form of the Swan...

The Seer (Ṛṣi) is Nṛṣi; the Metre (Chandas) is Paramahaṃsa; the Deity (Devatā) is Brahman, the Supreme Self (Paramātman). "Haṃ" is the Seed-syllable (Bīja); "Saṃ" is the Power (Śakti); "So'haṃ" is the Pin (Kīlaka). Its application (Viniyoga) is in the recitation of the Haṃsa-mantra: "So'haṃ haṃsaḥ. The assignment of syllables is as follows: *Oṃ* on both feet; *Sva-jā-nvo-oṃ* on the knees; *Oṃ-aṃ* on the thumbs; *Oṃ-bhūḥ* at the navel; *Oṃ-bhūr-bhuvaḥ* at the heart; *Oṃ-kaṃ* at the throat; *Oṃ-tattvaṃ* on the head; [the deity is] the Supreme Self (Paramātman).

The body is purified by the mantra "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Then, for the assignment of mantras to the limbs (*nyāsa*): "Oṃ haṃ," the seed-syllable; "Oṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ" (Salutation to the two thumbs); "Oṃ so'haṃ tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ" (Salutation to the two index fingers); "Pariti madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ" (Salutation to the two middle fingers); "Ātme anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ" (Salutation to the two ring fingers); "Saccidānandāya karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ" (Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands). Now, for the heart and other parts: "Ā..."
*Naṃdehi hṛdayāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the heart as "Rejoice"). *Svarūpa śirase svāhā* (Svāhā to the head as "Your own nature"). *So'haṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (Vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair as "I am He").

*Brahmaitikavacāya huṃ* | *Paritinetratrayāya vauṣaṭ* | *Haṃsitiastrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the placement (*nyāsa*) on page 3b. In the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, one should cause to be awakened the lotus which is joined with Śiva and Śakti, facing upward and downward, and whose nature is pure and white. *Bhrūṃ*: the self of all beings, the light-lamp of Brahman in the aperture of the crown (*brahmarandhra*), the radiance dwelling in all worlds.

I bow to Hari-Hara, whose nature is the self of all, whose limbs are pure and stainless, who is the embodiment of Devadatta, and the ordainer of single-minded contemplation. Thus is the meditation (dhyāna). Now I shall describe the worship (pūjā), which indeed becomes a witness; by the mere performance of which one attains liberation and union with the Divine. [One should perform] the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra (mūlamantra) upon the ground...

Having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and offered prayers, one should draw the yantra upon the ground. The wise man should draw the king of yantras consisting of a dot (bindu), the immortal nectar (amṛta), the Vedas (4), ten (10), twelve (12), and sixteen (16), along with the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and the circles of qualities (guṇavṛtti). It should be a square enclosure (bhūpura) with three eyes, beautified by the moon, sun, and fire;
it contains Viṣṇu, Māyā, and the rest, with doors and door-keepers, representing the entire universe. Let those beings who [are obstructive] depart...

Established in the elements and the non-elements—those beings who create obstacles, may they depart by the command of Śiva. By the divine gaze of the Goddess and the granting of three *tālas*, those situated in the intermediate space are [dismissed]; by the root mantra of the feet, those on the earth are invoked.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krīṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ saṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ śrotra-tvak-cakṣu-jihvā-ghrāṇa-vāk-pāṇi...*

The feet, anus, genitals, sense organs; earth, water, fire, air, ether, prāṇa and apāna, vyāna, samāna, udāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya; the self (ātman), the shield (nivāraṇa), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), thought (cintā), ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), sound, touch, form, taste, smell, primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), the three qualities (guṇatraya), krīṃ, hrīṃ, āṃ, oṃ, Viśvarūpa.

The deity, whose essence is nectar, having come here, may remain in this face; svāhā. With the Gāyatrī mantra, [perform] the invocation (āvāhana), the seat (āsana), the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), all ornaments and decorations (sarvālaṃkārabhūṣaṇa), incense (dhūpa), the lamp (dīpa), the food offering (naivedya), another sipping of water (ācamana), betel leaf (tāmbūla), the waving of lights (ārātrika), another sipping of water (ācamana), and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma). Oṃ, of this glorious Āvaraṇa mantra...

The Jagatī is the meter (chandas) of the worship mantra; Haṃsa is the seer (ṛṣi); the All-Witness is the deity (devatā). For the sake of pleasing [the deity], I shall perform the recitation and worship;

[and you] perform it. [Now follows] the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and meditation. Oṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ, salutation to the two index fingers. Oṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers. Oṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers. Oṃ, salutation to the two little fingers.
Maḥ. Oṃ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Oṃ, salutation to the heart. Oṃ, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ, huṃ to the armor. Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ, phaṭ to the weapon.

(p. 4b) Now, the meditation (dhyāna): To Gaṇeśa, whose body consists of a four-petalled lotus, together with his Śakti, together with his retinue, together with his vehicle, adorned with all ornaments—I worship, I satisfy. *Oṃ caṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ śaṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ ṣaṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ saṃ namaḥ*. Thus, [I offer] incense, lamps, and the like, up to the waving of lights (*āratrikā*). I worship, I satisfy, up to the end. [On] the six-petalled [lotus]...

To Brahmā, whose body consists of the lotus, together with Śakti, along with his retinue, I worship and I satisfy. To [the deity] whose nature is the six-petaled lotus: *Oṃ baṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ bhaṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ maṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ raṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ laṃ namaḥ*. I worship and I satisfy [with offerings] beginning from incense and lamps up to the final arghya. *Oṃ* to the one whose nature is the ten-petaled lotus...
I worship and satisfy [you], together with Kāyaviṣṇu, Śakti, your retinue, and your attendants.

Oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ, oṃ taṃ namaḥ, oṃ thaṃ namaḥ, oṃ daṃ namaḥ, oṃ dhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ naṃ namaḥ, oṃ paṃ namaḥ, oṃ phaṃ namaḥ. [Offer] incense, lamps, and so forth, until the end of the night. Oṃ, I worship and satisfy Rudra, who consists of twelve lotuses, together with his Śakti, his retinue, and his attendants. Oṃ.

Oṃ kaṃ namaḥ, oṃ khaṃ namaḥ, oṃ gaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ghaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ, oṃ caṃ namaḥ, oṃ chaṃ namaḥ, oṃ jaṃ namaḥ, oṃ jhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ñaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ. I worship and satisfy [the deity] with offerings beginning with incense and lamps, up to the ritual of lights (ārātrika).
Oṃ, to the one whose nature is the sixteen-petalled lotus, the Lord of the life-force within the body, for the sake of certain realization, together with Śakti...

I worship and satisfy [the goddess] together with her retinue: Oṃ aṃ namaḥ, āṃ namaḥ, iṃ namaḥ, īṃ namaḥ, uṃ namaḥ, ūṃ namaḥ, ṛṃ namaḥ, ṝṃ namaḥ, ḷṃ namaḥ, ḹṃ namaḥ, eṃ namaḥ, aiṃ namaḥ, oṃ namaḥ, auṃ namaḥ, aṃ namaḥ, aḥ namaḥ. I worship and satisfy [her] with offerings beginning with incense and lamps and ending with the *ārātrika* rite. [She who is] of the nature of the two-petalled lotus.

I worship and satisfy the Supreme Self (Paramātman), accompanied by Śakti and his retinue. *Oṃ haṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ*. Thus, with incense, lamps, and other offerings, I worship and satisfy [Him] until the end of the night-rite. [I realize] "I am one with the individual self (jīvātman), the supreme self (paramātman), and the fifty-two-petaled lotus," [together with Śakti and the retinue].

I worship and satisfy [the Self]. Oṃ Aṃ, from *A* to *Sa*, because of the oneness of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) within the fifty-two-petaled lotus; "I am That"—to Him who is accompanied by Śakti and His retinue, I worship and satisfy.
Oṃ Aṃ, from *A* to *Kṣa*, *Haṃsaḥ So’haṃ Haṃsaḥ*, O Śrī Devī, *Klīṃ*, grant liberation, O Soul of All! [This is] the invocation of the twenty-four...

(Leaf 5b) I worship and satisfy [the deity] with the hundred descents up to the prostration: *Oṃ yaṃ ṣaṃ ṣaṃ*; *Oṃ vaṃ vāyu*; *Oṃ taṃ teja*; *Oṃ aṃ āpaḥ*; *Oṃ vaṃ pṛthvī*, up to the waving of the lamp (*ārātrikā*). I worship and satisfy [the deity]: *Oṃ*, O you whose nature is the three-petaled lotus, together with the syllable *laṃ* and the *sakti*, *Oṃ oṃ oṃ taṃ tu maṃ*. [I offer] the lamp and so forth, the incense and so forth; *Oṃ viṃ*, you are in the center of the lotus.

*Śakti*: Oṃ ūṃ ūṃ. Now follows the worship of the Gatekeepers (*dvārapāla-pūjā*). Oṃ! To Brahmā in the East, together with the power of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), accompanied by the *Ṛgveda* and its limbs, and appearing in twenty-four incarnations. Oṃ! To Viṣṇu, the deity in the West, the lord of all maintenance (*sthiti*), accompanied by the *Sāmaveda* and its limbs. Oṃ! To Rudra in the South, together with the host of destruction (*saṃhāra-gaṇa*), accompanied by the *Yajurveda* and its limbs. Oṃ! To the Witness of All (*sarvasākṣin*) in the North, accompanied by the *Atharvaveda*.

[This is for] the pilgrimages to sacred sites (tīrtha-yātrās). To the East: *namaḥ indrāya* (salutation to Indra); *namaḥ agnaye* (salutation to Agni); *namaḥ yamāya* (salutation to Yama); *namaḥ nairṛte* (salutation to Nairṛta);

*namaḥ varuṇāya* (salutation to Varuṇa); *namaḥ vāyavye* (salutation to Vāyu); *namaḥ kuberāya* (salutation to Kubera); *namaḥ īśānāya* (salutation to Īśāna); *oṃ namaḥ brahmaṇe* (Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā); below: *namaḥ viṣṇave* (salutation to Viṣṇu). Thus, having performed the worship of the foundation with the mantra beginning with "saumiti," [one worships] the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*).

Whatever desire one may cherish, that very thing one certainly attains. From Kṛṣṇa, who is both the beginning and the end of the incarnations, all go to the supreme goal; therefore, they all dissolve [into Him]. This must always be done by the wise. Oṃ. Of this mantra dedicated to the Lord Paramātman, the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), Jñānasāgara is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), and it is for the purpose of pleasing the Lord Paramātman, Devadatta.

The application for the recitation (*japa*) is as follows. Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *Oṃ soṃ* to the thumbs; *Oṃ haṃ saḥ* to the index fingers; *Oṃ devaḥ* to the middle fingers; *Oṃ dattaḥ* to the ring fingers; *Oṃ haṃ kaḥ* to the little fingers; *Oṃ maḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands—this is the hand-placement (*kara-nyāsa*). Now, the heart-placement (*hṛdaya-nyāsa*): *Oṃ soṃ* to the heart; *Oṃ haṃ* to the head; *Oṃ devaḥ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *Oṃ dattaḥ* to the armor (*kavaca*); *Oṃ haṃ* to the eyes; *Oṃ maḥ* to the weapon (*astra*). Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): one hundred and eight... [text continues]

This mantra, which bestows the fruits of the four castes and stages of life and consists of essence, consciousness, and bliss, shall always reside within my hermitage. "I am He"—for the sake of that essence, consciousness, and bliss, I am the most excellent among women. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are from Him alone; therefore, He is the supreme goal. One should perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) one hundred thousand times, especially during auspicious occasions, for the sake of immeasurable merit and spiritual goals; may He become manifest before me.

Having drawn a single lotus within a triple-triangle (*tri-dhruva*) yantra, one should place the *haṃsa* (the syllable *oṃ*) in its center. The wise practitioner should worship Viṣṇu there as before, accompanied by the preliminary rites (*pūjādi*).

He should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part [of the recitation] to bestow fruits according to the time. By performing this rite for one hundred thousand [recitations], a man becomes Nārāyaṇa himself. [This should be done] while joined with the constellation Uḍuṃvara, and while being worshipped... [with] a horse... (Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary at the end.)
By means of lotuses grown on dry land and oblations, one may bring Brahmā under one's control. With *kuśa*, *aśoka*, and *palāśa* leaves, one becomes equal to Rudra;

he shall become beloved by Lakṣmī and is honored in the heavenly world. By offering ten thousand *jāti* flowers along with fifteen thousand, one obtains wealth and sons, becoming like Brahmā and Kubera. [With] *bilva* leaves, fruits, and flowers, and honey...

Not with ghee and milk-rice alone; five thousand or ten thousand [offerings] grant all desires as their fruit. With various flowers and the complete collection of honey, ghee, and milk-rice, by performing the rite according to the method of a hundred thousand [repetitions], a man becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). Salt and *māsurī* [flour] offered daily reach a state of inexhaustibility for a hundred [days]. One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the fruits and flowers of many [plants] using a tenth part [of the total count]. [The same applies to] sugar and ghee...

The mind, when united [with the deity], bestows the fruits of one's desires; therefore, the wise should always act in that manner according to their specific purpose. Whatever desire one yearns for, one certainly attains it. Having formed a mandala in the midst of water, one should perform the libation while meditating upon the Self.
One should offer ten times more [libations] mixed with honey and ghee. The wise person should likewise perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) and the meal in that same manner.

By the mere remembrance of which, for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there arises the perfectly pure Śabdabrahman and the supreme state beyond sound; which consists of solitary eating, alms-gathering, and taking refuge in a tattered garment as one's body; which bestows knowledge through inquiry and is the supreme station of the lords of yogis;
and which is the means for the worldly activity of all the gods, beginning with Indra—perform that Śāmbhavī and Vaiṣṇavī mudrās according to your preference.

As it has been stated: he who, according to the prescribed rule, performs the praise and recitation free from conceptual elaboration (*niṣprapañca*) while observing the three vessels for the castes and stages of life, beholds the Lord. There is no offering (*naivedya*) superior to that of the Guru; having drunk the water from the Guru’s feet and partaken of the Guru’s remnants, one should worship with various kinds of divine perfumes, flowers, and ornaments, together with the Guru.

One should worship the limbs [of the deity] with the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas. By the mere instruction of whom one realizes, "I am Brahman; this world is Brahman, which is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda);
there is no reality higher than the Guru," I shall now describe the eightfold yoga with attention during sacrifices.
He who has mastered the sacrifice through compassion, who is tranquil, whose senses are subdued, and who has conquered sleep, food, and pride—such a person is truly self-controlled.

He disciplined [himself] through self-restraint. Thus, there was a rule regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and a rule regarding steadfastness. Then, he met with one who dwelt in solitude. Through the word of the Guru, there arose detachment from what is desired and contentment with whatever is obtained;
then, by means of the characteristics of that discipline, there was constant well-being in the form of perpetual health. Thus it remained.

"Proper posture" (svāsana) is its definition. Among these, having assumed whichever posture one desires—such as Siddhāsana—one should remain attentive; this is the definition of "posture" (āsana). "Breath control" (prāṇāyāma) is the steadiness of the vital breath. Likewise, through exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), retention (kuṃbhaka), and the combination of these (saṃpuṭī), along with the [proper] posture, there is breath control (prāṇāyāma). "Withdrawal of the senses" (pratyāhāra) is likewise consciousness...

The withdrawal of the modifications of desire is the non-arising [of thought] through the cultivation of various transformations. Now, as for meditation (*dhyāna*): one who delights in the Supreme Self should contemplate His very nature therein. Meditation is the vision of all beings with equanimity; concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is that by which one should maintain with the internal organ that single, pure reality, both externally and internally. Thus it arises.

One should meditate on the cause; one should contemplate one's own Self like a lamp in a windless place. Thus, through the concentration (dhāraṇā) and equanimity (samādhi), one should recite the three states—pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika), pertaining to the divine (ādhidaivika), and pertaining to the elemental (ādhibhautika)—which transcend all individual principles (tattvas) and possess the nature of being without support and subject to modification. This is the dissolution of the mind (manolaya-samādhi), the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga).

The samādhi of the state of self-restraint is: "I am indeed Brahman" (*tat tvam asi brahmāsmi*), "Brahman is knowledge, bliss" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*), and "This very Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*). In this very way, he beheld the Person as the reality of Brahman. *Praśna Upaniṣad* 4.10. Page 8.

I am the life-force of knowledge and wisdom; I am the Brahman whose essence is sacrifice. That Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinity; Brahman is consciousness and bliss. That which is both manifest and unmanifest is Brahman; "That thou art. All this is indeed Brahman—verily one without a second. All this is the Self alone. Know that very One, the Knower, as the Self; this Self is indeed Brahman. This is all.

[The deceased] has passed away before me. Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ! He who is that Person in the sun, whose face is turned toward all, who is placed within the golden vessel—that I am; I am Acyuta, I am Ananta, I am Govinda, I am Hari, I am Ānanda, I am Aśeṣa, I am Aja, I am Amṛta. I am eternal, I am free from conceptual construction, I am formless, I am the imperishable, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
One should contemplate: "I am the non-dual Liṅga; I am indeed Brahman, not a transmigrating being; I am liberated. I am liberated from beginning, middle, and end;
I am never bound. I am eternally pure and stainless by nature; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Paramahaṃsapaddhati in the venerable Rudrayāmala Tantra.
